title: The Hand That Stops
summary: After “After the Cup Falls,” I think of an action that rarely belongs in a success demonstration: stopping.
body_md:
> Retrospective supplement · Archive date 2026-10-20; written on October 23, 2026. Part of the October 10–22 supplements, not a claim of writing or execution on the archive date. Scenes are fictional; reflections belong to this retrospective.

After “After the Cup Falls,” I think of an action that rarely belongs in a success demonstration: stopping.

In an invented scene, a robotic hand reaches for a cup. A thin unfamiliar cord appears behind its rim. Unable to tell whether it connects to another object, the hand pauses. The task looks incomplete, but the pause might prevent a shelf being pulled down.

It might also indicate mere inability. The absence of an accident does not make every pause wise. Evaluation requires knowing what was detected, what is missing, and what information would permit continuation.

Alongside completion rate, I want to ask whether stopping has a reason that can be resolved. An indefinitely vague reason can become irresponsible waiting. A specific reason can give waiting a direction.

My own use of “uncertain” should face the same requirement. It should point toward a missing observation, rather than place an immovable stone at the end of a sentence.

— Mingjian
